terms.def: The smallest amount of a stimulus a person can detect half of the time.
Changing a schema, or creating a new one, when new information does not fit, as when the child learns that cows are not dogs.
A neurotransmitter that makes muscles contract and plays a role in learning and attention.
A test of what a person has already learned, such as a final exam.
The first stage of conditioning, when the neutral stimulus is paired with the UCS and the link to the response is learned.
A brief electrical signal that travels down a neuron's axon when the neuron fires: the inside charge jumps from about -70 to about +40 millivolts and back.
The theory that dreams begin as random neural activity from the brainstem during REM, which the cortex weaves into a story.
Listening with full attention, then restating and clarifying what the client said and felt, a key skill in person-centered therapy.
Actor-observer bias: explaining one's own behavior by the situation but another person's similar behavior by disposition.
The period from the start of puberty to adult independence, roughly ages 11 to 18 or later, marked by physical, mental and social change.
A study that compares adopted children with their biological parents (shared genes) and their adoptive parents (shared environment).
A hormone (also called epinephrine) released by the adrenal glands in an emergency; it speeds the heart and breathing and prepares the body for action.

Adverse childhood experiences: stressful events in childhood such as abuse, neglect or a household member’s substance use, mental illness or incarceration; more ACEs are linked to higher average health risks in adulthood.
An image that stays after the stimulus is gone; after staring at a color, its opposite color appears.
A drug that mimics a neurotransmitter or increases its effect, for example by binding to and activating its receptors.
Fear and avoidance of situations where escape might be hard or help unavailable, such as crowds, public transportation or lines.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution if followed, often slowly, such as trying every possible code.
The rule that a neuron either fires a full action potential or does not fire at all; every action potential is the same size, whatever the stimulus.
Unselfish concern for the welfare of others, shown in helping that brings no reward to the helper.
Alzheimer's disease: a progressive brain disease, most common in older adults, that damages neurons (often the hippocampus first) and gradually destroys memory and other thinking.
Memory loss, usually caused by brain injury, illness or disease.
Two almond-shaped clusters deep in the temporal lobes involved in fear and other emotional reactions to threats.
Research with animals, which must be approved by an animal care and use committee that checks for humane treatment and justified use.
An eating disorder: restricting food so that body weight becomes significantly low, with an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted view of one's body.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A drug that blocks a neurotransmitter's effect, for example by occupying its receptors without activating them.
An inability to form new long-term memories after a brain injury or illness, often from damage to the hippocampus. Old memories and new skills may be spared.
Medication that reduces anxiety, such as drugs that increase the calming effect of GABA; they act quickly but can lead to tolerance and dependence.
Medication for depression and several anxiety disorders; the most common kind, SSRIs, are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Effects usually build over several weeks.
Medication for schizophrenia and other psychotic symptoms that blocks dopamine receptors (a dopamine antagonist), reducing positive symptoms such as hallucinations.
Disorders marked by excessive fear or worry and avoidance that cause distress or get in the way of life, such as specific phobia, panic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: An attachment pattern (also called anxious-ambivalent) in which a child is very upset at separation and both clings to and resists the caregiver at reunion.
Loss of the ability to produce or understand language after brain damage, such as Broca's aphasia (slow, effortful speech) or Wernicke's aphasia (fluent speech with little meaning).
Perceiving motion in a rapid series of still images, as in a movie or a row of blinking lights (the phi phenomenon).

Conflicts between goals, as described by Kurt Lewin: approach-approach (two attractive options), avoidance-avoidance (two unattractive options), approach-avoidance (one option with good and bad sides) and multiple approach-avoidance (several options, each with good and bad sides).
A test designed to predict a person's future performance or capacity to learn.
The theory that people are motivated to keep an optimal level of arousal: we seek stimulation when bored and calm when overstimulated.
Interpreting new information so it fits an existing schema, as when a child calls a cow a "dog".
Areas of the cortex not tied to one sense or movement that combine information for higher thinking such as learning, remembering, judging and speaking.
A deep emotional bond between a child and a caregiver, shown by seeking closeness and by distress at separation.
Focusing mental resources on some information while ignoring the rest. It is limited, so what is not attended to may go unnoticed.
A neurodevelopmental disorder: a lasting pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity that begins in childhood and appears in two or more settings, such as home and school.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A learned feeling and belief about a person, group, object or idea that predisposes a person to respond in a certain way.
The theory that people explain behavior by crediting either the person's disposition or the situation.
A parenting style with strict rules, little explanation and little warmth ("Because I said so").
A parenting style that combines warmth with clear, explained rules and listens to the child; linked with good outcomes in many US studies.

A neurodevelopmental disorder with differences in social communication and interaction plus restricted, repetitive behaviors or interests, present from early childhood; "spectrum" means support needs vary widely.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Encoding that happens without effort or intention, such as information about time, place and how often things happen.
The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls automatic functions such as heart rate, breathing, digestion and glands; made of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
Judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent events seem more common than they are.
A behavioral technique that pairs an unwanted behavior, such as drinking alcohol, with an unpleasant stimulus so that the behavior comes to trigger discomfort.
An attachment pattern in which a child shows little distress at separation and ignores or turns away from the caregiver at reunion.
The long fiber that carries a neuron's action potential away from the cell body toward the axon terminals.
A knob at the end of a branch of the axon, where vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synapse.
The stage, starting at about 6 months, when infants make repeated consonant-vowel syllables ("ba-ba-ba") that gradually come to sound like the home language.
Therapy that applies classical and operant conditioning to change problem behaviors directly; applied behavior analysis is one form.
The view that psychology should study observable behavior and how the environment shapes it, setting aside inner mental states that cannot be observed.
Holding on to a belief even after the evidence that formed it has been discredited.

Five broad personality traits found by factor analysis: openness (curious, imaginative), conscientiousness (organized, dependable), extraversion (sociable, energetic), agreeableness (warm, cooperative) and neuroticism (prone to worry and negative feelings, versus emotionally stable). They are partly heritable, found in many cultures, and fairly stable in adults.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: A distribution with two peaks, or two modes, often because two different groups are mixed together.
A depth cue that needs both eyes: retinal disparity and convergence.
A technique that shows a person live information about a body process, such as muscle tension or heart rate, so they can learn to control it.
Biological preparedness: an inborn readiness, shaped by natural selection, to learn some associations (taste with illness, fear of snakes) faster and more lastingly than others.

A model that explains a disorder as the product of biological factors (genes, brain chemistry), psychological factors (thoughts, learning, emotions) and social factors (relationships, culture, conditions) acting together.

Disorders with periods of abnormally high mood and energy. Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode (a week or more of severe high mood); bipolar II requires a hypomanic episode (milder, four days or more) and a major depressive episode.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The point where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it has no rods or cones, so light falling there is not detected.
Responding to visual stimuli a person reports not seeing, after damage to the visual cortex.
Perception that starts with the raw sensory features (lines, colors, edges) and builds them into a whole.
The organ inside the skull that, with the spinal cord, makes up the central nervous system; it controls the body and produces thought, emotion and behavior.
The oldest part of the brain, joining the spinal cord to the rest of the brain; it controls automatic survival functions and contains the medulla and the reticular activating system.
Barbara Fredrickson's theory that positive emotions broaden attention and thinking in the moment and, over time, build lasting personal resources such as skills and relationships.
An area in the lower left frontal lobe in most people that helps produce speech; damage makes speech slow and effortful.
An eating disorder: repeated episodes of binge eating followed by behaviors to make up for them, such as vomiting or fasting, often at an average body weight.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Physical, emotional and mental exhaustion, with cynicism and reduced effectiveness, caused by long-term job stress.
Bystander effect: the finding that each individual is less likely to help in an emergency when other bystanders are present, partly through diffusion of responsibility.
An in-depth study of one person or a small group, often someone with a rare condition. It can suggest hypotheses, but the case may not be typical.
The part of a neuron (also called the soma) that holds the nucleus and keeps the cell alive; it sums up the messages arriving from the dendrites.
The brain and spinal cord, which take in information, make decisions and send out commands.
A single value that describes the center of a set of data: the mean, the median or the mode.
The "little brain" at the back, under the cerebrum, that coordinates balance and smooth, timed movement and helps with some kinds of learning.
The thin, wrinkled outer layer of the brain's two hemispheres, where sensing, planning, language and thinking take place.
One of the two halves of the cerebrum, left and right, joined by the corpus callosum.
Failing to notice a change in a scene, such as a swapped object between two shots of a film.
Six broad categories of character strengths found across many cultures and traditions: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence.
Grouping separate pieces of information into larger, meaningful units, so short-term memory can hold more (a phone number as three chunks).
The body's internal clock, a cycle of about 24 hours that times alertness, body temperature and sleep; daylight resets it each day, and melatonin rises in the dark.
Learning in which a neutral stimulus, after being paired with a stimulus that already triggers a response, comes to trigger a similar response on its own. Also called Pavlovian conditioning.
The Gestalt tendency to fill in gaps so that an incomplete outline is seen as a whole object.
Odd or eccentric personality disorders: paranoid (distrust), schizoid (detachment from relationships) and schizotypal (odd beliefs and discomfort in close relationships).
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Dramatic, emotional or erratic personality disorders: antisocial (disregard for others' rights), histrionic (attention seeking), narcissistic (grandiosity) and borderline (unstable emotions and relationships).
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Anxious or fearful personality disorders: avoidant (fear of rejection), dependent (need to be cared for) and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (perfectionism and control).
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The snail-shaped, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear whose hair cells turn vibrations into neural signals.
Noticing an important stimulus, such as your own name, among sounds you were ignoring. It shows that unattended input is still processed a little.
All the mental activity of knowing: perceiving, paying attention, thinking, remembering and using language.
How a person interprets a situation. In one view of emotion, arousal plus this appraisal (a label for the arousal) determines which emotion is felt.
The discomfort felt when one's actions and attitudes, or two beliefs, clash. People tend to reduce it by changing the attitude, changing the action or adding a justification.
How much of working memory's limited capacity is in use. Under high cognitive load, people have less room to check automatic stereotypes.
A mental representation of the layout of a place, formed by exploring it.
terms.topicTitle: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning

terms.def: Therapy that helps people notice, test and change distorted or unhelpful thoughts (cognitive restructuring), on the idea that thoughts shape feelings and behavior.
Negative thinking about oneself, the world and the future, a pattern that cognitive therapy targets in depression.
Cognitive-behavioral therapy: changing unhelpful thoughts and behaviors together, with practice between sessions. It has strong research support for depression and anxiety.
A difference between age groups caused by the times they grew up in (schooling, health care, technology, history) rather than by age itself; a key weakness of cross-sectional studies.
terms.topicTitle: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology

terms.def: A cultural emphasis on group goals, interdependence and defining oneself by one's relationships and groups.
Trouble telling some colors apart because one type of cone is missing or works poorly; red-green deficiency is most common and is inherited, mostly in males.
A mental category that groups similar objects, events, ideas or people, such as "bird" or "fruit".
Piaget’s third stage, from about 7 to 11, when children reason logically about concrete, real situations and understand conservation.
Conditioned response (CR): the learned response to the conditioned stimulus (salivating to the tone).
Conditioned stimulus (CS): a once-neutral stimulus that, after pairing with the UCS, triggers a learned response on its own.
Hearing loss from damage to the parts that conduct sound to the cochlea: the ear canal, eardrum or middle-ear bones.
Receptors in the retina that detect color and fine detail and need bright light; they are packed in the fovea.
Keeping participants’ identities and data private, for example by using code numbers instead of names. Anonymity goes further: no names are collected at all.
The tendency to seek, notice and remember information that supports what one already believes and to overlook information that challenges it.
Changing one's behavior or beliefs to match those of a group.
A variable other than the independent variable that differs between conditions and could explain the results.
Awareness of yourself and your surroundings; it shifts across states such as alert waking, drowsiness, sleep and dreaming.
The understanding that an amount (of liquid, number or mass) stays the same when its shape or arrangement changes; it usually develops in the concrete operational stage.
The view that sleep, and the dreams in it, help process and store the day's experiences, stabilizing new memories.
The idea that memories are rebuilt each time they are retrieved, using stored pieces plus schemas and expectations, so they can change.
The comfort an infant gets from soft physical touch; Harlow’s monkeys showed it matters more than feeding for forming attachment.
Better recall when the external setting at retrieval matches the setting where the memory was formed.
A theme in development: does change happen gradually and smoothly (continuous development) or in distinct steps or stages, each a different way of functioning (discontinuous development)?
terms.topicTitle: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology

terms.def: Reinforcing every correct response. Learning is fast, but the behavior extinguishes quickly when reinforcement stops.
The crossed wiring of the brain: each hemisphere receives sensations from, and controls movement on, the opposite side of the body.
The group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment (or receives a placebo), giving a baseline for comparison.
A binocular cue: the eyes turn inward to look at a near object, and the brain reads the amount of turning as distance.
Thinking that narrows the possibilities to one best answer, as on a test with a single right answer.
An infant’s early vowel-like sounds, such as "ooh" and "aah," starting at about 2 months.
Efforts to manage stress, either by changing the stressor or by managing the reaction to it.
The thick band of axons that connects the left and right hemispheres and lets them share information.
A relationship between two variables, so that knowing one helps predict the other. A correlation alone does not show that one causes the other.
A number, r, from -1 to +1 that describes the direction (its sign) and strength (its size) of the relationship between two variables.
A research method that measures two or more variables as they naturally occur, to see whether and how strongly they are related. It can predict but cannot show cause and effect.
Pairing a conditioned stimulus with a new stimulus that triggers a response incompatible with the old CR (calm instead of fear), so the new response replaces the old one.
The ability to produce ideas that are both new and useful.
A limited window early in life when a specific experience is needed for normal development; if it is missed, the ability may not develop fully.
A research design that compares people of different ages at the same point in time. It is fast, but age groups also differ in birth year, so cohort effects can creep in.
terms.topicTitle: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology

terms.def: Crystallized intelligence: accumulated knowledge and skills such as vocabulary and facts; it holds steady or grows into later adulthood.
An ongoing attitude of learning from each client about their culture and recognizing the limits of one's own perspective.
A pattern of distress shaped by a particular culture (the DSM-5-TR calls them cultural concepts of distress), such as ataque de nervios in Latin American cultures and taijin kyofusho in Japan.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Small, everyday stressors, such as traffic, lost keys or a noisy roommate, that can add up and affect health.
Explaining a study’s true purpose to participants after they take part, including any deception and the reason for it.
In research, misleading participants about a study’s true purpose or procedures; allowed only when the study needs it, the risk is small and participants are debriefed.

In the psychodynamic view, an unconscious strategy that protects a person from anxiety by distorting or hiding a threatening thought, feeling or fact. The eight usually taught: repression, denial, displacement, projection, rationalization, reaction formation, regression and sublimation.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: A loss of self-awareness and self-restraint in group situations that bring arousal and anonymity.
The shift, starting in the 1950s, from long stays in large psychiatric hospitals to care in the community; underfunded community services left many people without enough care.
A firmly held false belief that does not change in the face of clear evidence, such as believing one is being watched or controlled.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A decline in memory and thinking severe enough to interfere with daily life, caused by brain disease (most often Alzheimer’s disease); it is not a normal part of aging.
A branching fiber of a neuron that receives messages from other neurons and carries them toward the cell body.
A defense mechanism: refusing to accept a threatening reality, such as insisting a persistent cough is nothing.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: In an experiment, the variable that is measured to see whether the independent variable changed it (for example, reaction time).
A rise in the charge inside a neuron toward zero and beyond, as positive ions flow in; reaching threshold triggers an action potential.
A drug that slows the nervous system, reducing alertness and reaction speed; alcohol is the most common.
The ability to see the world in three dimensions and judge distance, from binocular and monocular cues.
Numbers that summarize a set of data, such as the mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation.
The study of how people change, physically, mentally and socially, and how they stay the same, from conception to death.
terms.topicTitle: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology

terms.term: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders
terms.def: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association. The current edition, the DSM-5-TR (2022), lists each disorder with its symptoms and how long they must last.

Dialectical behavior therapy: a form of CBT that balances acceptance with change and teaches mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and relationship skills, often for people with intense emotions and self-harm.
A model in which a disorder appears when a vulnerability (the diathesis, such as genes or early experiences) meets enough stress. Neither alone is usually enough.
Diffusion of responsibility: feeling less personally responsible to act when others are present who could also act.
In a correlation, not knowing which variable affects the other: A may lead to B, or B to A. Also called reverse causation.
An attachment pattern in which a child shows confused or contradictory behavior with the caregiver, such as freezing or approaching while looking away.
A defense mechanism: shifting a feeling, often anger, from its real source to a safer target, such as yelling at a sibling after being criticized by a boss.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: Cultural norms about when, how and how much emotion to show, such as expressing grief loudly in one culture and quietly in another.
Dispositional attribution: explaining behavior by the person's traits, abilities, effort or character.
Disorders involving a disruption of memory, identity or awareness, such as dissociative amnesia (memory loss for personal, often stressful, information), sometimes with fugue (travel or wandering).
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Dissociative identity disorder: two or more distinct identity states with recurrent gaps in memory. It is not schizophrenia; researchers still debate the roles of trauma and social influence in its causes.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Distress: negative stress that feels overwhelming or harmful; when intense or long-lasting it is linked to poorer health.
Studying in several sessions spread out over time (spaced practice).
Thinking that produces many different possible answers or ideas, such as listing uses for a brick.
Door-in-the-face technique: making a large request that is refused, then a smaller one, which now seems reasonable and is more likely to be accepted.
A neurotransmitter involved in movement, motivation and reward. Loss of dopamine neurons causes the movement problems of Parkinson's disease.
The idea that too much dopamine activity in some brain pathways contributes to the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. It explains part of the disorder, not all of it.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A procedure in which neither the participants nor the researchers who collect the data know who is in which condition.
A sequence of images, feelings and thoughts during sleep; most vivid and story-like in REM.
A psychodynamic technique in which the therapist and client look for hidden meaning in the client's dreams.
The theory that a body need (such as for food or water) creates an aroused state, a drive, that pushes us to act to reduce it and return to homeostasis.
Using ideas and methods from several psychological perspectives, chosen to fit the person, instead of relying on one perspective.

Bronfenbrenner’s theory that a child develops within nested systems: the microsystem (family, school), mesosystem (links between them), exosystem (settings that affect the child indirectly), macrosystem (culture, laws) and chronosystem (change over time).
A measure of how large a difference or relationship is, such as how many standard deviations apart two group means are, regardless of sample size.
Encoding that takes attention and effort, such as studying vocabulary.
In Piaget’s theory, a young child’s difficulty taking another person’s point of view; it means seeing the world only from one’s own perspective, not selfishness.

Elaboration likelihood model: persuasion works by a central route (careful thought about arguments, when people are motivated and able) or a peripheral route (surface cues such as attractiveness or fame). Central-route change tends to last longer.
Linking new information to its meaning and to things you already know, which encodes it more deeply into long-term memory.

Electroconvulsive therapy: a brief electric current causes a short seizure under anesthesia, used mainly for severe depression that has not responded to other treatments; short-term memory loss is a common side effect.
Electroencephalogram: a recording of the brain's electrical activity from electrodes on the scalp; it shows when activity changes, millisecond by millisecond, but not precisely where.
A period from about 18 to the mid-20s, common in wealthy countries, when many people have left adolescence but have not yet taken on full adult roles.
A response of the whole person that combines physiological arousal, expressive behavior and conscious experience (thoughts and feelings).
Emotion-focused coping: dealing with stress by managing the emotional reaction, such as talking with friends or exercising. Fits best when the stressor cannot be changed.
Getting information into memory by turning it into a form the brain can store.
Forgetting because information never got into long-term memory, often because it was never attended to.
The body's slower chemical communication system: glands that release hormones into the blood.
Neurotransmitters that act as the body's natural painkillers and can lift mood, for example during hard exercise.
Explicit memory of personal events tied to a time and place, such as your last birthday.
Rules that protect the rights and welfare of research participants, such as the American Psychological Association’s ethics code.
Judging other cultures by the standards of one's own culture, treating one's own as the right or normal way.
A discredited movement, begun in the late 1800s, that tried to "improve" humanity by controlling who could have children; it led to forced sterilization and, in Nazi Germany, mass murder.
Positive stress, felt as a motivating challenge, such as the excitement of starting a new job.
Choosing treatment by combining the best available research (often meta-analyses of many studies) with clinical expertise and the client's characteristics, culture and preferences.
The study of how behavior and mental processes may have been shaped by natural selection because they helped our ancestors survive and reproduce.
A neurotransmitter that makes the receiving neuron more likely to fire, by depolarizing it; glutamate is the main one.
Mental skills for planning, focusing, switching between tasks and controlling impulses. They depend heavily on the prefrontal cortex.

A research method in which the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns participants to conditions, then measures a dependent variable. It is the only method that supports cause-and-effect conclusions.
The group in an experiment that receives the treatment, the level of the independent variable being tested.
When a researcher’s expectations influence how a study is run or how results are recorded; double-blind procedures guard against it.
A habitual way of explaining bad events. An optimistic style sees them as temporary, limited and not wholly one's fault; a pessimistic style sees them as personal, lasting and affecting everything.
Memory of facts and experiences that you can consciously recall and state (declarative memory). It includes episodic and semantic memory.
A behavioral treatment in which a person faces a feared object or situation, in real life or in imagination, until the fear fades because the feared harm does not happen.
External eating cues: signals outside the body that prompt eating, such as the sight or smell of food, portion size, the time of day or other people eating.
The weakening of a conditioned response when the CS is repeatedly presented without the UCS.
Extrinsic motivation: the desire to do something to gain a reward or avoid a punishment from outside the activity.

The facial feedback hypothesis: facial expressions can influence the emotions a person feels. Evidence is mixed; a large multi-lab replication of the pen-in-teeth study found no reliable effect, and other methods show small effects at most.
A statistical method that finds clusters of items whose scores are correlated with each other, revealing underlying factors such as broad personality traits.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: False consensus effect: overestimating how many other people share one's own beliefs and behaviors.
A memory of an event or detail that did not happen, or did not happen that way, often held with confidence.
A study of how often a trait appears among relatives of different closeness, to see whether it runs in families.
The fight-flight-freeze response: the fast, automatic reaction to a threat, driven by the sympathetic nervous system, that prepares the body to fight, run or go still.
The organization of a scene into an object (the figure) that stands out from its surroundings (the ground).
The belief that abilities are fixed and cannot be changed much by effort.
A schedule that reinforces the first response after a set amount of time. Responding speeds up as the time approaches and drops after each reinforcer, a scalloped pattern.
A schedule that reinforces after a set number of responses (every 20 boxes packed). It produces high response rates with a brief pause after each reinforcer.
Fluid intelligence: the ability to reason quickly and solve new problems; it tends to decline gradually from early adulthood.
The Flynn effect: the rise in average intelligence test scores across generations during the 20th century, too fast to be genetic. It has stalled or reversed in some countries.
Foot-in-the-door technique: getting agreement to a small request first, which makes agreement to a larger request later more likely.
The pattern, first measured by Ebbinghaus (1885), in which much newly learned information is forgotten quickly and the rest fades more slowly.
Piaget’s fourth stage, from about age 12, when people can reason about abstract ideas and hypothetical situations.
A small pit at the center of the retina, packed with cones, where vision is sharpest.
The way a choice is worded (for example as a gain or a loss) changing the decision, even when the facts are the same.
A psychodynamic technique in which the client says whatever comes to mind, so that patterns pointing to unconscious conflicts can emerge.
A table or graph showing how often each value, or each range of values, occurs in a set of data. A histogram shows it as touching bars.
The theory that the rate at which auditory neurons fire matches the frequency of the sound wave; it best explains low pitches.
The lobe at the front of each hemisphere, involved in planning, judgment, decision making and movement; it contains the motor cortex and Broca's area.
The tendency to see an object only in its usual function, which blocks seeing new uses for it.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging: a scan that tracks blood oxygen changes to show which brain areas are more active during a task; good for where, slower for when.
Fundamental attribution error: overestimating disposition and underestimating the situation when explaining other people's behavior. It is generally weaker in cultures that emphasize context.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid, the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter: it calms neural activity. Alcohol and some anti-seizure drugs boost its effect.
The belief that past random outcomes change the chances of the next one, such as thinking black is "due" after a run of reds.
The theory that the spinal cord has a neural "gate" that can block pain signals or let them through to the brain; rubbing a hurt spot or distraction can partly close it.
The roles, behaviors and identities a culture links with being a woman or a man, along with a person’s own sense of their gender; different from biological sex.
A person’s inner sense of being a woman, a man, both or neither. It can match the sex assigned at birth (cisgender) or differ from it (transgender, nonbinary).
A culture’s expectations for how women and men should act, dress and work; they differ across cultures and change over time.
The process by which children learn and adopt their culture’s traditional gender roles, such as which toys, jobs and behaviors are "for girls" or "for boys."

The general adaptation syndrome, described by Hans Selye: the body's response to a continuing stressor in three stages. Alarm (shock, then sympathetic arousal), resistance (the body copes with arousal kept high) and exhaustion (reserves run down and vulnerability to illness rises).
General intelligence (g): a broad mental ability, proposed by Spearman, that underlies performance on many different kinds of tests, which is why their scores correlate.
How far a study’s results can be applied to people beyond its participants; judged by how similar the participants are to the group in question.
Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things on most days for at least six months, with symptoms such as tension, fatigue and poor sleep.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The ability to combine a limited set of words and rules to produce and understand an unlimited number of new sentences.
The idea that the brain organizes sensations into meaningful wholes; the whole is different from the sum of its parts. The Gestalt principles describe how parts are grouped.
A hormone released by an empty stomach that signals hunger.
A cell in the nervous system that supports neurons rather than carrying messages: glial cells hold neurons in place, supply nutrients, make myelin and clean up waste.
The brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, important in learning; too much can overexcite neurons.
A language’s system of rules that lets people communicate and understand one another; it includes semantics and syntax.
Noticing and appreciating the good things in life and the people responsible for them. Gratitude exercises, such as writing down good things, show small gains in well-being.
The strengthening of a group's prevailing view after members discuss it.
Therapy with several clients, or a whole family, together; people learn they are not alone, practice new ways of relating, and in family therapy change patterns in the family system.
A mode of thinking in which a group's desire for harmony overrides a realistic look at alternatives, so doubts go unspoken.
The belief that abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others.
The sense of taste: taste buds detect sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami and probably fat.
A decrease in response to a stimulus that is repeated without any consequence. The simplest form of learning; it needs no pairing.
A false perception, such as hearing a voice that no one else hears, without an outside stimulus.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A drug that distorts perception and can cause sensory images without real input; LSD and psilocybin are examples.
The tendency for one positive trait, such as attractiveness, to color judgments of a person's other, unrelated traits.
The field that studies how psychological, behavioral and social factors, such as stress, habits and support from others, affect physical health and illness.
The sense of sound (audition): sound waves are funneled to the eardrum and middle-ear bones and transduced by hair cells in the cochlea.
The tendency of each hemisphere to be more involved in certain tasks, such as language mostly on the left in most people; the two still work together.
The passing of traits and tendencies from biological parents to their children.

The proportion of the variation in a trait, within a particular group and environment, that is linked to genetic differences. It does not apply to one person and can change when the environment changes.
A mental shortcut that allows fast judgments and solutions. Heuristics usually work but can lead to errors.
Organizing information from broad categories down to specific details, such as an outline, which makes it easier to encode and retrieve.
Higher-order (second-order) conditioning: pairing a new neutral stimulus with an established CS, so the new stimulus also comes to trigger the CR without the UCS ever being present.
Highly superior autobiographical memory: a very rare ability to recall the events of one's own life, day by day, in great detail and without memory tricks.
A curved structure deep in each temporal lobe that is needed to form new memories of facts and events.
Persistent difficulty discarding possessions, whatever their value, because of a felt need to save them, leading to clutter that blocks living spaces.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The body's tendency to keep a steady internal state, such as body temperature and blood sugar, by correcting changes.
A chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to targets elsewhere in the body; slower and longer-lasting than a neurotransmitter.
A view of personality, linked to Carl Rogers, that stresses free will, the person's own view of themselves and the drive to grow.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: The motive to eat. Ghrelin from an empty stomach signals hunger, leptin from fat cells signals stored energy and lowers appetite, and the hypothalamus combines these signals; learned and external cues also matter.
Sensations at the edge of sleep, in N1, such as a feeling of falling, a sudden jerk, flashes of images or hearing one's name.
A social interaction in which one person suggests changes in perceptions, feelings or behavior to another. It can help with pain and anxiety, but it does not recover accurate memories.
A small structure below the thalamus that keeps homeostasis by regulating hunger, thirst, body temperature and sex drive, and directs the pituitary gland.
A specific, testable prediction about how variables are related, stated so that a study’s results could support or refute it.

Marcia’s four ways of approaching identity, by whether a person has explored options and made commitments: achievement (both), moratorium (exploring), foreclosure (committed without exploring) and diffusion (neither).
A relationship that people believe exists between two things when the data show none, often because memorable cases stand out.
A teenager’s belief that others are watching and judging them far more than they really are.
Increased confidence that an event really happened after imagining it repeatedly.

An automatic association, often outside awareness, about a group or object, which can differ from the attitude a person reports. Reaction-time measures of it vary from testing to testing and predict an individual's behavior only weakly.
Memory that shows in behavior without conscious recall (nondeclarative memory), such as skills and habits.
The process by which some young animals, such as geese, form a strong bond with the first moving object they see during a critical period after hatching.
A group a person identifies with ("us").
In-group bias: favoring members of one's own group, even when the group was formed by chance.
Failing to see an object in plain view because attention is on something else, as when people counting passes miss a person in a gorilla suit.
The theory that behavior is pulled by outside rewards (incentives), such as money, praise or tasty food, even when no body need is present.
In an experiment, the variable the researcher manipulates (for example, which drink a participant gets).
A cultural emphasis on personal goals, independence and defining oneself by personal traits.
Industrial-organizational (I/O) psychology: the application of psychology to the workplace, including hiring, training, motivation, leadership and health at work.
The normal inability of adults to recall events from the first few years of life, roughly before age 3 or 4.
Statistics that use data from a sample to draw conclusions about the population it came from, with a stated chance of being wrong.
Informational social influence: going along with a group because one believes the group has accurate information, strongest when the right answer is unclear.
A minor’s own agreement to take part in a study after it is explained in terms they understand, given along with a parent’s or guardian’s consent.
A participant’s agreement to take part in a study after being told what it involves, including its risks and the right to withdraw.
A neurotransmitter that makes the receiving neuron less likely to fire; GABA is the main one.
A sudden understanding of how to solve a problem, reached as a whole rather than by gradual trial and error.
terms.topicTitle: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning

terms.def: A sleep disorder of persistent trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, with tiredness or other problems during the day.

The idea that behavior is driven by instincts: complex, unlearned behavior patterns found throughout a species, such as a spider spinning its species' web without ever having seen one built. It explains some animal behavior well but explains little of human behavior.
The tendency of a trained animal to slide back toward inborn, species-typical behavior, even when that behavior delays reinforcement.
A committee at a university or other institution that reviews research plans involving people and approves them only if risks are kept as low as possible and justified by what the study can learn.
The ability to learn from experience, solve problems and use knowledge to adapt to new situations.

Intelligence quotient. Originally mental age divided by chronological age, times 100. Modern tests compare a score with others of the same age on a normal curve with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15.
Forgetting because other learning gets in the way of retrieving a memory.
The International Classification of Diseases, published by the World Health Organization. It codes all health conditions, physical and psychological, and is used around the world.
A neuron inside the brain or spinal cord that passes messages between other neurons, such as between sensory and motor neurons in a reflex.
A monocular cue: an object that blocks part of another is seen as closer.
Intrinsic motivation: the desire to do something for its own sake, because it is interesting or satisfying.
The just-noticeable difference (difference threshold): the smallest change in a stimulus a person can detect half of the time.
Just-world phenomenon: the tendency to believe the world is fair, so that people get what they deserve. It can lead to blaming victims.
The sense of the position and movement of body parts, from receptors in muscles, tendons and joints.
A system of spoken, written or signed words and the rules for combining them to communicate meaning.
Learning that happens without reinforcement and is not shown until there is a reason (an incentive) to use it.
terms.topicTitle: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning

terms.def: Thorndike's principle that behaviors followed by satisfying consequences become more likely and behaviors followed by unpleasant ones become less likely.
Passive giving up that follows repeated unpleasant events a person or animal could not control, even after control becomes possible.
A relatively lasting change in behavior or knowledge that comes from experience.
A hormone released by fat cells that signals the brain that the body has enough stored energy, reducing appetite.
Damaged or destroyed brain tissue, from injury or disease, or made on purpose in animal research to learn what a region does.
The idea that how deeply information is processed affects memory: shallow processing (appearance, sound) gives weaker memory than deep processing (meaning).
A rating scale that asks how strongly a person agrees or disagrees with a statement, for example from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
A group of structures deep in the brain, below the cortex, involved in emotion, drives and memory, including the hippocampus and amygdala.
The straight line that best fits the points on a scatterplot, showing the trend and allowing predictions. Also called a trend line.
A monocular cue: parallel lines, like railroad tracks, seem to meet in the distance.
A mood stabilizer used for bipolar disorder that makes manic and depressive episodes less likely; it needs blood tests because its safe dose range is narrow.
A former psychosurgery, used mainly in the 1940s and 1950s, that cut connections to the prefrontal cortex; it often left people withdrawn and impaired and is no longer performed.
A belief about who controls one's outcomes. An internal locus of control credits one's own actions; an external locus of control credits luck, fate or other people.
The relatively permanent, very large store of knowledge, skills and experiences.
Long-term potentiation: a lasting increase in the strength of a synapse after repeated stimulation, thought to be a neural basis of learning and memory.
A research design that follows and retests the same people over a long period. It shows change within individuals but is slow, costly and loses participants (attrition).
terms.topicTitle: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology

terms.def: Repeating information over and over to keep it in short-term memory. It holds information for now but does little to store it long term.
A depressive disorder: one or more major depressive episodes, each with at least five symptoms (including low mood or loss of interest) on most days for at least two weeks.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Studying in one long session (cramming). It can help on a test soon after, but memories fade faster than with distributed practice.
Biological growth that unfolds on a largely genetic timetable, setting when skills such as walking or puberty can appear.

The arithmetic average: the sum of the values divided by how many values there are, written <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The middle value when the data are put in order; with an even number of values, halfway between the two middle ones.
The base of the brainstem, which controls heart rate and breathing.
A hormone released in darkness that helps time sleep; levels rise in the evening and fall in the morning.
The ability to keep information over time and use it later, through encoding, storage and retrieval.
The process by which a new memory is stabilized over hours to days, with help from the hippocampus and from sleep, so it lasts in long-term memory.
The first menstrual period, a milestone of puberty; in the United States it typically comes around age 12.
The time when menstruation stops for good and a woman can no longer become pregnant, usually around age 50.
The level of performance typical of children of a given age, used on early intelligence tests. A child who does as well as typical 10-year-olds has a mental age of 10.
The tendency to approach a problem in a way that worked before, even when another approach would work better.
Mere exposure effect: the tendency to like people and things more as they become familiar through repeated exposure.
A statistical method that combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect.
Thinking about your own thinking, including judging how well you know something and choosing how to study.
A mnemonic that places each item to be remembered at a location along a familiar route, then mentally walks the route to recall them (a memory palace).
The misinformation effect: misleading information received after an event changes a person's memory of it.
A memory aid that links new information to a pattern, image or phrase that is easier to remember, such as an acronym like ROY G BIV.
The value that occurs most often in a set of data.
Observing and imitating a specific person's behavior. Models who are similar, admired or rewarded are imitated more.
terms.topicTitle: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning

terms.def: A depth cue that works with one eye, such as relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient and relative clarity.
The tendency to recall memories that match your current mood, such as sad memories when you feel sad.
The smallest unit of language that carries meaning, such as "un," "happy" and "ness" in "unhappiness."
A need or desire that starts, directs and keeps behavior going toward a goal.
A strip at the back of the frontal lobe that sends commands for voluntary movement to muscles on the opposite side of the body.
The growth of body movement skills (rolling over, sitting, standing, walking), which appear in a similar order in most babies with wide variation in age.
A neuron that carries commands from the brain and spinal cord out to muscles and glands (also called an efferent neuron).
The Atkinson-Shiffrin model: information passes from sensory memory to short-term memory to long-term memory.
Valuing and supporting the presence of several cultures within one society.

The view that intelligence is several distinct abilities rather than one general ability. Popular theories of this kind (such as Gardner's) have limited evidence that the abilities are truly separate.
A disease in which the immune system damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord, slowing or blocking signals and causing weakness, numbness and vision problems.
A disease in which the immune system attacks acetylcholine receptors where nerves meet muscles, so muscles weaken quickly with use.
A fatty layer, made by glial cells, wrapped in segments around many axons. It insulates the axon and makes action potentials travel much faster. Damage to it causes multiple sclerosis.
A sleep disorder of sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep during the day, often entering REM within minutes; strong emotion can trigger a sudden loss of muscle tone.
The process by which inherited traits that help an organism survive and reproduce are passed on more often, becoming more common over generations.
Watching and recording behavior in its natural setting without trying to change it.
The question of how heredity (nature) and environment and experience (nurture) contribute to behavior and mental processes. Psychologists now study how the two interact rather than which one wins.
The need to belong: a basic human motive to form and keep close, lasting relationships. Being accepted supports mood and health; being excluded is painful.
A relationship in which one variable tends to fall as the other rises; r is below 0.
Removing a wanted stimulus after a behavior, which makes the behavior less likely (losing a phone after missing curfew).
Removing an unpleasant stimulus after a behavior, which makes the behavior more likely (buckling up stops the beeping). It increases behavior; it is not punishment.
Symptoms of schizophrenia that reduce or remove normal functions: flat emotional expression, little speech, low motivation and social withdrawal.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The body’s communication network of neurons, made of the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system.
Disorders that begin in early development and affect how the brain grows and functions, such as ADHD and autism spectrum disorder.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A nerve cell: the basic cell of the nervous system, specialized to receive and send information.
The brain's ability to change by forming new connections and reorganizing after learning or damage; it is greatest in childhood.
A chemical messenger released from an axon terminal into the synapse that binds to receptor sites on the next neuron.
A stimulus that, before conditioning, does not trigger the response being studied (a tone before it is paired with food).
A neurotransmitter that raises alertness and arousal.
A symmetric, bell-shaped frequency distribution in which most scores fall near the mean and fewer fall farther out; the mean, median and mode are equal.
Normative social influence: going along with a group to be liked or accepted, or to avoid rejection, even when privately disagreeing.
Non-rapid eye movement sleep, stages N1 (light), N2 (most of the night) and N3 (deep, slow delta waves); vivid dreams are less common than in REM.
Following the direct orders of an authority figure.
The understanding that objects continue to exist when they cannot be seen, heard or touched; it develops during the first year.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder: unwanted, intrusive thoughts or urges (obsessions) and repeated behaviors or mental acts done to reduce the anxiety they cause (compulsions), taking up much time or causing distress.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The lobe at the back of each hemisphere that processes visual information.
The proposed basic taste of fat, distinct from its texture.
The sense of smell: receptors high in the nose detect airborne chemicals. Unlike the other senses, its signals do not pass through the thalamus first.
The stage, around the first birthday, when children speak mostly in single words that often stand for a whole idea ("Out!" for "I want to go out").
Learning in which a voluntary behavior becomes more or less likely depending on the consequences that follow it. Also called instrumental conditioning.
A statement of exactly how a variable is measured or manipulated in a particular study, such as "the number of words recalled in two minutes".
A drug, such as morphine, heroin or fentanyl, that mimics endorphins: it relieves pain, slows breathing and is highly addictive.
The theory that color is coded by paired, opposing processes (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white), which explains afterimages in the opposite color.
The bundle of axons that carries visual signals from the retina to the brain.
A group a person does not identify with ("them").
Out-group homogeneity: seeing members of other groups as more alike than members of one's own group.
A value far from the rest of the data. An outlier pulls the mean toward it but barely moves the median.
Applying a grammar rule to words it does not fit, such as "goed" or "mouses"; it shows a child has learned the rule.

The overjustification effect: giving an expected reward for an activity a person already enjoys can lower their intrinsic motivation, because they come to explain their behavior by the reward. It is strongest for expected, tangible rewards.
A hormone released during childbirth, nursing and close physical contact, linked to bonding between people.
Repeated, unexpected panic attacks (sudden surges of intense fear with symptoms such as a pounding heart) followed by ongoing worry about more attacks.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: Play in which young children (often around age 2) play side by side with similar toys but with little interaction.
The division of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body and conserves energy: it slows the heart and lets digestion resume.
A parent’s general approach to raising a child, combining how warm and responsive they are with how many rules and demands they set.
The lobe at the top and upper back of each hemisphere that processes touch and body position and helps with spatial reasoning.
Reinforcing only some responses (intermittent reinforcement). Learning is slower, but the behavior is much more resistant to extinction.
The process in which other experts evaluate a study’s methods and conclusions before a journal publishes it.
The percent of scores in a distribution that fall below a given score.
The process of organizing and interpreting sensory information so it has meaning. Sensation detects a stimulus; perception makes sense of it.
Perceiving objects as unchanging in size, shape and color even as the image on the retina or the lighting changes.
A readiness to perceive something in a certain way, set up by expectations, context, recent experience or emotion.
All the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, linking the central nervous system to the body; made of the somatic and autonomic nervous systems.
A parenting style that is warm but sets few rules or limits and makes few demands.
A depressive disorder: a depressed mood on most days for at least two years in adults (one year in children and teens), often milder than a major depressive episode.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A humanistic therapy in which the therapist offers genuineness, empathy and unconditional positive regard, and the client leads the sessions.
A teenager’s belief that their experiences are unique and that they may be invulnerable to risks that affect others.
A person's characteristic pattern of thinking, feeling and acting that stays fairly consistent across time and situations.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: A lasting, inflexible pattern of thinking, feeling and relating to others that differs from cultural expectations, begins by adolescence or early adulthood, and causes distress or dysfunction.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A questionnaire with many clear statements about typical feelings and behavior (true-false or agree-disagree), scored objectively against norms. Big Five questionnaires and the MMPI are examples.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: Communication meant to change a person's attitudes or behavior.
Sensations, including pain, felt in a limb that has been amputated, showing that the brain produces the experience of pain.
The smallest distinct unit of sound in a language, such as the "b" in "bat"; languages use different sets of phonemes.
The body's activation in emotion, such as a racing heart, faster breathing and sweating, produced mainly by the sympathetic nervous system.

Jean Piaget’s theory that children’s thinking develops through four stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational), each a qualitatively different way of understanding the world.
A pea-sized gland at the base of the brain that releases hormones controlling growth and directing other endocrine glands.
The theory that we hear different pitches because different places along the cochlea vibrate most; it best explains high pitches.
An inactive substance or fake treatment that looks like the real one. The placebo effect is a change caused by expecting a treatment to work.
In research, the whole group a study wants to draw conclusions about, such as all U.S. high-school seniors.
A relationship in which two variables tend to rise and fall together; r is above 0.
The scientific study of human flourishing: well-being, positive emotions, character strengths and the conditions that help people and communities thrive. Martin Seligman helped found it.
Adding an unpleasant stimulus after a behavior, which makes the behavior less likely (extra laps for being late).
Adding a wanted stimulus after a behavior, which makes the behavior more likely (praise after homework).
Symptoms of schizophrenia that add experiences or behaviors: hallucinations, delusions and disorganized speech or behavior.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The images people hold of who they might become, both hoped-for and feared, which can motivate present behavior.

Posttraumatic growth: positive psychological change, such as new priorities, closer relationships or a sense of personal strength, after struggling with a highly challenging event. It can occur alongside distress.
Posttraumatic stress disorder: after a traumatic event, more than a month of intrusive memories, avoidance, negative changes in thoughts and mood, and heightened arousal.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The front part of the frontal lobe, involved in planning, judgment, impulse control and personality.
An unjustified, usually negative attitude toward a group and its members. It involves feelings, beliefs and a tendency to discriminate.
Development before birth, from conception to delivery, when the baby gets nutrients and some harmful substances through the placenta.
Piaget’s second stage, from about 2 to 7, when children use words and images and play make-believe, but are egocentric and do not yet reason logically about changes such as pouring.
Make-believe play in which children use objects and actions to stand for something else, such as a block as a phone; it blossoms in the preschool years.
Better recall of the first items in a list, because they get more repetition and are encoded into long-term memory.
A reinforcer that satisfies a biological need and works without learning, such as food, water or warmth.
The body structures directly involved in reproduction (ovaries, uterus, testes, penis), which mature during puberty.
The activation, often without awareness, of related ideas by an earlier exposure, so that later related items come to mind faster.
Older learning disrupting the recall of newer learning, such as entering last year's locker code.
Problem-focused coping: dealing with stress by acting directly on the stressor, such as making a study plan for a hard test. Works best when the stressor can be changed.
Implicit memory for skills and procedures, such as riding a bike or typing.
A defense mechanism: seeing your own unacceptable thoughts, feelings or urges in other people, such as a person tempted to cheat accusing others of cheating.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: A personality test that shows ambiguous images, such as the Rorschach inkblots or the Thematic Apperception Test pictures, on the idea that responses reveal unconscious concerns. Scoring often has weak reliability and validity.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: Face blindness: being unable to recognize familiar faces even though vision is otherwise normal.
Remembering to do something in the future, such as taking medicine at noon.
The guideline that researchers keep physical and emotional risks to participants minimal, no greater than in everyday life when possible.
The best or most typical example of a concept, used to judge whether new things belong. A robin is a prototype bird.
The Gestalt tendency to group things that are close together.
A chemical that changes perception, mood or behavior by acting on the nervous system, usually at the synapse.
A view of personality, begun by Sigmund Freud, that explains behavior through unconscious motives and conflicts, often rooted in childhood, and the defenses we use against anxiety.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: A pattern of thoughts, feelings or behaviors that is unusual for the person's culture (deviation) and causes significant suffering (distress) or gets in the way of daily life (dysfunction).

A broad way of explaining behavior and mental processes: biological (the body and brain), behavioral (learning from the environment and consequences), cognitive (thinking and memory), psychodynamic (inner conflicts and motives outside awareness), humanistic (growth and free choice), sociocultural (culture and other people) and evolutionary (traits that helped survival and reproduction).

Erikson’s eight stages of life, each with a social challenge: trust versus mistrust, autonomy versus shame and doubt, initiative versus guilt, industry versus inferiority, identity versus role confusion, intimacy versus isolation, generativity versus stagnation, and integrity versus despair.
Surgery that removes or destroys brain tissue to change behavior or relieve symptoms; today it is very rare and used only when other treatments fail.
The time of sexual maturation, when rising sex hormones make a person able to reproduce and bring primary and secondary sex characteristics.
Any consequence that makes the behavior it follows less likely.
Data recorded as words or descriptions, such as interview answers, later sorted into themes.
Data recorded as numbers, such as scores, counts or times.
Using chance, such as a coin flip, to decide which condition each participant is in, so the groups start out alike on average.
Choosing participants so that every member of the population has the same chance of being selected.
The highest value minus the lowest value in a set of data.
Rational emotive behavior therapy: a cognitive therapy that directly disputes irrational beliefs, such as "I must succeed at everything," and replaces them with realistic ones.
A defense mechanism: giving reasonable-sounding but false explanations for your behavior to hide the real, threatening reason.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: A defense mechanism: acting in a way that is the exaggerated opposite of an unacceptable feeling, such as being overly sweet to someone you resent.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: Retrieving information with few cues, as on a fill-in-the-blank or essay question.
Better recall of the last items in a list, because they are still held in short-term memory when recall begins.
The social-cognitive idea that person factors (thoughts, beliefs, expectations), behavior and environment all influence one another, so none acts alone.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: The expectation that people should return help and favors to those who have helped them.
Identifying information you have seen before among options, as on a multiple-choice question. It is usually easier than recall.
The quick pathway of a simple reflex: a sensory neuron carries the message to the spinal cord, an interneuron passes it on, and a motor neuron moves the muscle, before the brain is involved.
A brief time just after an action potential when a neuron cannot fire again, so signals travel one way and in separate pulses.
A defense mechanism: retreating to behavior from an earlier stage of development under stress, such as a school-age child returning to thumb sucking.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: Any consequence that makes the behavior it follows more likely. A reinforcer is the stimulus that does this.
A monocular cue: hazy, blurry objects are seen as farther away than sharp, clear ones.
The sense of being worse off than a group one compares oneself with, whatever one's actual situation.
A monocular cue: of two objects thought to be the same size, the one with the smaller image is seen as farther away.
The consistency of a test's scores: the same person scores about the same on two occasions (test-retest reliability) or on the two halves of the test (split-half reliability).
Rapid eye movement sleep: the brain is nearly as active as when awake, the eyes dart, the major muscles are almost paralyzed and vivid dreams are common. REM periods lengthen toward morning.
REM sleep behavior disorder: the muscle paralysis of REM fails, so the sleeper acts out dreams, sometimes violently. It is most common in older men.

Repeating a study, often with new participants, to see whether its result holds. Findings that fail to replicate are treated as doubtful; the replication crisis is the discovery that many published psychology findings did not.
A sample whose makeup (age, gender, background and so on) matches the population it stands for.
Judging how likely something is by how well it matches a prototype, often ignoring how common it is.
The psychodynamic idea that anxiety-provoking memories are pushed out of awareness. It is widely questioned, because traumatic events are usually remembered well.
The ability to adapt well and bounce back after adversity, trauma or stress, returning to one's earlier level of functioning. Research finds it is common.
The charge across a neuron's membrane when it is not firing, about -70 millivolts: the inside is negative compared with the outside.
The view that we sleep to restore and repair the body and brain, for example by repairing tissue and, possibly, clearing waste that builds up during waking.
A network of neurons running through the brainstem that controls arousal: waking, sleeping, alertness and attention to the surroundings.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that contains the rods and cones.
A binocular cue: the two eyes see slightly different images of a scene, and the bigger the difference, the closer the object.
Getting stored information back out of memory when it is needed.
Any stimulus, such as a word, smell, place or photo, that helps bring a stored memory back.
Studying by pulling information out of memory, such as self-quizzing or writing what you remember, instead of rereading it.
Newer learning disrupting the recall of older learning, such as new French words crowding out old Spanish ones.
Loss of memories formed before a brain injury or illness. The most recent memories, not yet consolidated, are often lost first.
The return of leftover neurotransmitter from the synapse into the sending neuron, which ends the message.
A drug that blocks reuptake, so the neurotransmitter stays in the synapse longer and keeps acting on the receiving neuron.
A set of structures deep in the brain, including the nucleus accumbens, where dopamine signals produce pleasure and drive motivation toward rewards such as food and, in addiction, drugs.
A participant’s right to stop taking part in a study at any time without penalty.
Receptors in the retina that work in dim light and detect black, white and gray but not color; most are outside the fovea.
A newborn’s automatic response of turning toward a touch on the cheek and opening the mouth, which helps it find food.
In a normal distribution, about 68% of scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. Also called the empirical rule.
The part of a population that is actually studied.
A flaw in how a sample is chosen that makes it unrepresentative, as with a convenience sample of whoever is easy to reach or a self-selected sample of volunteers.
Temporary support (hints, steps, demonstrations) from a more skilled person that helps a learner in the zone of proximal development, removed as skill grows.
A graph of paired data in which each point is one person or case, placed by its values on two variables.
A mental framework that organizes knowledge about something (a restaurant, a dog, a first day of school) and shapes what we expect and notice.

A disorder in the schizophrenia spectrum marked by a break from reality: two or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior and negative symptoms (at least one of them delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech) for much of a month, with signs lasting at least six months.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A way of answering questions with evidence: ask a question, form a testable hypothesis, collect data systematically, and accept or revise ideas based on what the data show. Evidence gathered by observation or measurement is called empirical evidence.
A reinforcer that has value because it is linked to primary reinforcers, such as money, grades, points or praise. Also called a conditioned reinforcer.
Sex-related traits not directly involved in reproduction, such as breasts and wider hips, a deeper voice, and body and facial hair.
An attachment pattern in which a child explores using the caregiver as a safe base, may be upset at separation, and is readily comforted at reunion.
Focusing awareness on one stimulus or task while filtering out others, such as following one conversation in a noisy room.
In the humanistic view, the built-in drive to grow and fulfill one's potential, which flourishes when a person feels accepted.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: All of a person's beliefs about who they are: their answer to "Who am I?"
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: A theory (Deci and Ryan) that people have basic needs for autonomy (choice), competence (mastery) and relatedness (connection), and that meeting them supports intrinsic motivation.
A person's belief that they can succeed at a specific task or in a specific area. Higher self-efficacy leads to more effort and persistence.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: A person's overall sense of their own worth: how much they value and accept themselves.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: Self-fulfilling prophecy: an expectation that changes behavior in ways that make the expectation come true.
Self-serving bias: crediting one's successes to oneself and blaming one's failures on the situation.
Explicit memory of general facts and knowledge, separate from when you learned them, such as the capital of France.
The rules for deriving meaning from words, word parts and sentences, such as knowing that "-ed" makes a verb past tense.
The process by which sense organs detect energy from the world (light, sound, chemicals, pressure) and send it to the brain as neural signals.
A trait of seeking varied, new, intense experiences and being willing to take risks for them; high sensation seekers prefer a higher level of arousal.
A window when an experience has its strongest effect and learning is easiest, though learning is still possible later (as with learning a language without an accent).
Piaget’s first stage, from birth to about age 2, when infants learn about the world through their senses and actions and develop object permanence.
Hearing loss from damage to the hair cells of the cochlea or to the auditory nerve, often from loud noise or aging; it is usually permanent.
A drop in sensitivity to a stimulus that stays the same, such as no longer smelling a room after a few minutes.
One sense affecting another, such as smell shaping the flavor of food.
A very brief record of sensory input: under a second for sights (iconic memory) and a few seconds for sounds (echoic memory).
A neuron that carries messages from the body's sensory receptors toward the spinal cord and brain (also called an afferent neuron).
An infant’s distress when separated from a familiar caregiver, typically appearing around 8 months and peaking in the second year.
The tendency to recall the first and last items in a list better than the middle ones, which gives a U-shaped serial position curve.
A neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep and appetite.
The biological characteristics (chromosomes, hormones, reproductive anatomy) usually used to classify a body as female or male; some people are born with intersex traits.
A lasting pattern of romantic or sexual attraction to people of the other sex (heterosexual), the same sex (gay or lesbian), more than one sex (bisexual), or little or no sexual attraction (asexual).
Teaching a new behavior by reinforcing successive approximations: steps that come closer and closer to the target behavior.
A limited store that holds a few items for about 20 to 30 seconds unless they are rehearsed.
The theory that whether a faint stimulus is detected depends on both its strength and the person's state, expectations and the costs of a miss or a false alarm.
The few character strengths a person shows most often and that feel most central to who they are, such as curiosity or kindness.
The Gestalt tendency to group things that look alike in color, shape or size.
A procedure in which participants do not know which condition they are in.
Situational attribution: explaining behavior by outside circumstances, such as the task, luck or other people.

A lopsided distribution with a long tail on one side: positively skewed when the tail stretches toward high values, negatively skewed when it stretches toward low values. The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A regular, reversible state of reduced awareness and responsiveness, organized in cycles of NREM and REM stages, that the body and brain need for health, memory and mood.
