A sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, briefly waking the person to breathe; loud snoring and daytime sleepiness are common.
Intense fear of social situations in which one might be watched or judged, with fear of embarrassment and avoidance.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: A culture’s expected timing for life events such as leaving home, marriage, parenthood and retirement.
Judging one's own abilities and situation against other people. Upward social comparison is with people who are better off; downward social comparison is with people who are worse off.
The tendency to answer questions in a way that makes oneself look good (social desirability bias), the main form of self-report bias, which distorts what people say about themselves.
Improved performance on simple or well-learned tasks in the presence of others; on hard or new tasks, others' presence tends to impair performance.

Social learning theory (observational learning): learning by watching others and imitating them. It depends on attention, memory (retention), the ability to reproduce the behavior and the motivation to do so.
terms.topicTitle: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning

terms.def: The tendency to put in less effort on a group task when individual contributions are pooled and not identified.
An unwritten rule for expected behavior in a group or situation (facing forward in an elevator).
Social responsibility norm: the expectation that people should help those who depend on them, without expecting anything in return.
A set of norms for how a person in a given position should act (student, coach, guard).
A situation in which each person pursuing self-interest leads to an outcome that is worse for everyone (overusing a shared resource).

A view of personality, developed by Albert Bandura, that explains behavior through the interaction of a person's thoughts and beliefs, their behavior and their environment, including what they learn by watching others.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: The part of the peripheral nervous system that controls voluntary movement of the skeletal muscles and carries sensations from the body.
A strip at the front of the parietal lobe, just behind the motor cortex, that registers touch, temperature and pain from the opposite side of the body.
Sleepwalking: walking or doing other actions while in deep N3 sleep, usually early in the night, with no memory of it later; more common in children.
Remembering information but forgetting, or mistaking, where it came from (source misattribution).
The finding that study spread out over time leads to better long-term retention than the same amount of study done all at once.
Intense, lasting fear of a particular object or situation, such as heights or spiders, out of proportion to the real danger, usually with avoidance.
terms.topicTitle: Selection of Categories of Psychological Disorders

terms.def: The first ejaculation, a milestone of puberty in boys, typically around age 13 or 14.
The column of nerve tissue inside the backbone that carries messages between the brain and the body; part of the central nervous system.
A condition in which the corpus callosum has been cut, usually to treat severe epilepsy, so the two hemispheres cannot share information directly.
The return of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest period, usually weaker than before.
A theme in development: does a trait such as shyness stay steady in a person over time (stability), or does it shift as they grow (change)? Research usually finds some of each.
terms.topicTitle: Themes and Methods in Developmental Psychology

terms.def: A measure of variation: roughly the typical distance of the values from the mean. A larger standard deviation means more spread.
Giving a test in the same way to everyone and setting norms from a large, representative sample, so individual scores can be compared with them.
Better recall when your internal state (calm, sleepy, after caffeine or a drug) at retrieval matches your state when you learned.

A result is statistically significant when it would be unlikely to occur by chance alone if there were no real difference or relationship; psychologists usually require a probability (p value) below .05, written <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><mn>.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p < .05</annotation></semantics></math>.
A generalized belief about the members of a group, which may be partly accurate but is often overgeneralized and applied to individuals who do not fit it.
A small rise in performance when people are reminded of a negative stereotype about a different group they are compared with.
A drop in performance when people fear confirming a negative stereotype about their group. Early studies found large effects; later, larger studies suggest the effect is smaller and less consistent.
A drug that speeds up the nervous system, raising alertness and heart rate; examples are caffeine, nicotine, cocaine and amphetamines.
Learning to respond to the conditioned stimulus but not to similar stimuli that were never paired with the UCS.
The tendency for stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus to trigger the conditioned response too.
Keeping encoded information over time.

Ainsworth’s laboratory procedure in which a 1-year-old is briefly separated from and reunited with a caregiver in an unfamiliar room; the child’s behavior, especially at reunion, classifies attachment.
The process by which we appraise and respond to events (stressors) that we see as threatening or challenging. Our response depends partly on how we interpret the event and our ability to handle it.
An event or condition that triggers stress, from catastrophes and major life changes to daily hassles.
A person's own judgment of their happiness: how satisfied they are with life, plus the balance of pleasant over unpleasant feelings. Measured by self-report.
A defense mechanism: channeling an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity, such as turning aggressive urges into competitive sport.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: A neurotransmitter that carries pain signals in the spinal cord and brain.
Continuing a choice because of what has already been invested (money, time, effort) that cannot be recovered.
Superordinate goals: shared goals that require groups to cooperate and that reduce conflict between them.
Superstitious behavior: a behavior strengthened by accidental reinforcement, because a reward happened to follow it although the behavior did not cause the reward.
A person with many more taste buds than average who tastes some flavors, especially bitter ones, much more intensely.
A research method that asks many people to report their own attitudes, beliefs or behaviors, through questionnaires or interviews.
The division of the autonomic nervous system that arouses the body for action: it speeds the heart, widens the pupils, slows digestion and increases sweating.
The junction where the axon terminal of one neuron meets another neuron, including the tiny synaptic gap the neurotransmitter crosses.
A condition in which stimulating one sense also triggers another, such as seeing colors when hearing music or reading numbers.
The rules for combining words into grammatically sensible sentences, such as word order ("The dog bit the man").
A behavioral technique that pairs relaxation with a step-by-step list of feared situations, from least to most frightening, to countercondition the fear.
Involuntary, repeated movements of the face, lips and tongue that can develop after long-term use of antipsychotic medication, especially older ones.
A learned dislike of a food or taste after it was followed by illness. It can form after a single pairing, even with hours between the taste and the illness.
Early speech, around 18 to 24 months, that keeps key content words in the right order and leaves out small words ("Daddy go car"), like a telegram.
A person’s inborn, partly heritable style of emotional reactivity and activity, such as easygoing, fussy or slow to warm up, visible from infancy.
The lobe on the side of each hemisphere, below the lateral fissure, that processes hearing and contains Wernicke's area.
The tend-and-befriend response: under stress, protecting and caring for others (tend) and seeking social support (befriend). First described in women by Shelley Taylor and linked to oxytocin.
A substance or infection that can harm development before birth, such as alcohol, nicotine, some medicines and the rubella virus.
The finding that retrieving information, as on a practice test, strengthens long-term memory more than spending the same time restudying it.
A monocular cue: surface detail looks coarse and spread out up close and finer and denser in the distance.
The brain's sensory relay station: it routes signals from every sense except smell to the right areas of the cortex.
In science, a broad explanation that organizes many observations and predicts new ones. A theory is tested and revised, not a guess.
The understanding that other people have their own thoughts, feelings and beliefs, which can differ from one’s own and can be false; usually clear by age 4 to 5.
The bond of trust between a therapist and a client, with agreement on goals and on how to work toward them; a strong alliance predicts better outcomes across many therapies.
An outside variable that affects both of two correlated variables and may explain why they are related.
The level of charge, about -55 millivolts, that a neuron must reach to fire an action potential.
The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon: feeling sure you know something, and recalling parts of it such as the first letter, without being able to retrieve it yet.
An operant technique in which people earn tokens (secondary reinforcers) for target behaviors and trade them for rewards.
The need for a larger dose of a drug to get the same effect after repeated use, as the brain adapts to it.
Perception guided by knowledge, expectations and experience, such as reading a messy word from the sentence around it.
An approach that describes personality by stable tendencies (traits), such as being outgoing or careful, that show across many situations, rather than explaining where they come from.
terms.topicTitle: Social-Cognitive and Trait Theories of Personality

terms.def: Transcranial magnetic stimulation: magnetic pulses from a coil on the scalp stimulate targeted brain areas, used mainly for depression that has not responded to medication.
The conversion of one form of energy, such as light or sound waves, into neural signals by sensory receptor cells.
The theory that color vision depends on three types of cones, most sensitive to red, green or blue light, whose combined signals code every color.
A study that compares how alike identical twins (who share all their genes) and fraternal twins (who share about half) are on a trait, to estimate genetic influence.
The savory taste, detected by receptors for glutamate, found in broth, soy sauce, tomatoes and aged cheese.
Unconditional positive regard: accepting and valuing a person without conditions, even while judging a behavior. In the humanistic view it lets people see themselves honestly and grow.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: Unconditioned response (UCR): the unlearned, automatic response to the unconditioned stimulus (salivating to food).
Unconditioned stimulus (UCS): a stimulus that triggers a response naturally, with no learning (food, a puff of air, a loud noise).

In the psychodynamic view, the large part of mental life outside awareness: wishes, fears and memories that still influence behavior. Modern research supports unconscious processing in a narrower form, such as priming.
terms.topicTitle: Psychodynamic and Humanistic Theories of Personality

terms.def: Basic emotions, often listed as happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, whose facial expressions are recognized above chance across many cultures. Recognition is better within one's own culture, and how universal they are is still debated.
How well a test measures or predicts what it is meant to. Construct validity: it measures the intended trait. Predictive validity: its scores predict a later outcome, such as grades.
A schedule that reinforces the first response after an unpredictable amount of time (checking for new messages). It produces slow, steady responding.
A schedule that reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses (a slot machine). It produces the highest, steadiest response rates and the most resistance to extinction.
How spread out the values in a set of data are; measured by the range and the standard deviation.
The sense of balance and head movement, from fluid-filled canals and sacs in the inner ear.

Vicarious conditioning: learning from the consequences that happen to a model. Vicarious reinforcement (the model is rewarded) makes imitation more likely; vicarious punishment (the model is punished) makes it less likely.
terms.topicTitle: Social, Cognitive, and Neurological Factors in Learning

terms.def: The sense of sight: the eye focuses light on the retina, where rods and cones transduce it into neural signals sent to the occipital lobe.
A glass table with a shallow side and an apparent drop, used by Gibson and Walk (1960) to show that most crawling babies perceive depth and avoid the drop.
The volley principle: groups of auditory neurons take turns firing so that together they match a sound's frequency, extending frequency theory to middle pitches.
The principle that the just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, so a bigger stimulus needs a bigger change to be noticed.
An area in the upper back of the left temporal lobe in most people that helps understand language; damage leaves speech fluent but hard to understand.
The unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms that follow stopping a drug the body has adapted to.

Within-group variation is the spread of scores inside one group; between-group variation is the difference between groups' averages. A trait can be strongly heritable within groups while a gap between groups is caused by the environment.
A change in people’s answers caused by how a question is phrased.

The active part of short-term memory, where information is held and worked on. The model has a central executive (directs attention), a phonological loop (sounds and words) and a visuospatial sketchpad (images and places).

The finding that performance is best at a moderate level of arousal, falling when arousal is too low or too high. The best level is lower for difficult or new tasks and higher for simple or well-practiced ones.

How many standard deviations a score is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow><mtext>SD</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{\text{SD}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Also called a standard score.
Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development: the range of tasks a learner cannot yet do alone but can do with help from someone more skilled.
